Carrier loaded with Qatari LNG makes rare Red Sea journey to get gas to Europe

The transit, which comes as European natural gas prices hit highest level in 4 yrs, is unusual. Commercial vessels have increasingly tended to take long detours to avoid the Red Sea.

Stephen Stapczynski

19 October, 2026 06:34 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

QatarEnergy's LNG production facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, Qatar on 2 March 2026 | Reuters/File Photo

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

A carrier loaded with Qatari liquefied natural gas is sailing north through the Red Sea, potentially speeding up delivery to European customers with a rare transit through waters vulnerable to renewed attacks from Houthi rebels.

The tanker, which loaded an LNG cargo in Qatar in August, is signaling Poland as its next destination, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Poland’s Orlen SA has a long-term supply contract with QatarEnergy, though shipments under the deal were canceled after the exporter’s giant Ras Laffan plant was hit by drone strikes in March.

The transit — which comes as European natural gas prices hit the highest level in almost four years — is unusual. Commercial vessels have increasingly tended to take long detours to avoid the Red Sea, typically sailing around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope to head to Europe, a route that can add almost two weeks and extra costs to a one-way journey.

Show Full Article

UK Maritime Trade Operations, a security outfit which links commercial shipping and military forces, reported on Saturday that an unnamed LNG tanker was approached southeast of the Yemeni port of Al Mukalla, in the Gulf of Aden, by a skiff that fired two shots. The tanker’s security team fired two shots in return.

UKMTO did not provide further details, though ship-tracking data suggest the Poland-bound carrier was the only LNG tanker in the region at the time. The data suggests the vessel has since continued its journey.

QatarEnergy did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Continued disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has tightened global LNG supply for months, driving up prices and forcing Middle Eastern suppliers to look for workarounds.

This latest Qatari cargo is heading to Europe at a time when the continent has struggled to refill its gas inventories ahead of winter. Reserves of the fuel are sitting at the lowest seasonal level in over a decade, threatening even higher prices as temperatures begin to drop.

Elon Musk promises a SpaceX share to every child in the US next year

With roughly 72–73 million people under the age of 18 in the US, Musk’s one-time gift would be valued at about $10.5 to $10.7 billion as of now.

Himanshi Aggarwal

19 October, 2026 06:06 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

With roughly 72–73 million people under the age of 18 in the US, Musk’s one-time gift would be valued at about $10.5 to $10.7 billion as of now | X: Elon Musk

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Elon Musk has promised to distribute a share of SpaceX to each child in the United States of America next year. His announcement on X came hours after AI giant Anthropic detailed plans to dedicate a significant portion of its equity to serve the public.

“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” Musk wrote in a post on X.

SpaceX shares are currently trading at around $146-147. With roughly 72–73 million people under the age of 18 in the US, this one-time gift would be valued at approximately $10.5 to $10.7 billion according to current prices. However, Musk is yet to release details on eligibility, distribution mechanics, tax treatment, or any restrictions on the shares.

Show Full Article

SpaceX was founded by Musk in March 2002, and he currently holds a 48.4 per cent stake in the company, representing roughly 6.42 billion shares valued at over $860 billion to $900 billion.

Also read: France’s unrest reaches the Louvre as protesters block the iconic museum

Following Anthropic’s footsteps Musk’s charity pledge followed Anthropic’s announcement on Sunday, a day before his announcement.

Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, structured as a public benefit corporation, said it would commit 5 per cent of its shares (subject to stockholder approval) to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund.

“It will start off with 5 per cent of our shares. For every 50 per cent increase in the company’s value over a set baseline, we can contribute up to an extra 2 per cent, subject to our board’s discretion,” they wrote in a post detailing the scheme. “In total, this means that roughly 20 per cent of Anthropic’s shares are committed to public good.”

The post highlighted that the co-founders have already pledged to donate 80 per cent of their equity, and nearly half the employees are also donating a portion of their equity as part of a donation matching program. The company emphasized that none of the equity held by the fund will be used for lobbying or will be given to political parties.

“I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” Musk had written in response to Anthropic’s post adding , “This is what I will be doing.”

His follow-up post on Monday specified that children in the US would be the initial recipients of SpaceX equity.

The announcements arrive amid heightened scrutiny of AI companies over safety risks, job displacement, the environmental footprint of large-scale computing, and other concerns.

Despite the charitable pledge, Musk has a history of high-profile pledges that he does not follow through with, Bloomberg noted.

In October 2021, Musk challenged the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) to provide an open-source spending plan showing how $6 billion of his wealth could solve world hunger. When they gave him a breakdown, Musk did not follow through with his promise.

(Edited by Janaki Pande)

Israeli police arrest suspects over settler attacks on US journalist, European diplomats

Reuters

19 October, 2026 01:30 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

TEL AVIV, Oct 19 (Reuters) – Israeli police said on Monday they had arrested 10 suspects as part of an investigation into violent incidents in the occupied-West Bank over the weekend, including separate attacks on a Washington Post photojournalist and European diplomats.

The United States, Israel’s closest ally, had urged a crackdown on settler violence and the arrest of the perpetrators of the attack on the Washington Post photojournalist. France, Belgium and Poland, whose diplomats were attacked, also called on Israel to take action.

Police said the suspects were arrested in a pre-dawn operation on suspicion of involvement in acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order and illegal construction.

Show Full Article

The suspects, whom police did not identify, were taken into custody for questioning. Israel’s Army Radio reported that they were Israeli citizens.

Prosecutions of Israeli settlers are rare.

A video released by the police of the pre-dawn operation appeared to show at least one arrested suspect, whose face is not seen, wearing ritual tassels known as tzitzit, which are often worn by observant Jewish men.

The video also appeared to show two slingshots, which can be used to hurl stones, being found at one property. On Friday, when the Washington Post journalist was attacked, dozens of masked settlers, some armed, descended on a Palestinian olive harvest, with some settlers hurling stones with slingshots.

Police, military forces and the Shin Bet domestic security service took part in the operation.

Referring to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, Israeli police commissioner Daniel Levy said the law applied to everyone, “regardless of identity or affiliation”.

“The Israel Police is committed to professional, equal, and impartial law enforcement, based on evidence and in accordance with the law,” he said in a statement announcing the arrests.

MASKED SETTLERS

Masked Israeli settlers were filmed on Friday assaulting Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a US citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank. Levine was taken to hospital and underwent surgery on a finger.

On Saturday, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank. A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also damaged.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed “Israeli rioters” for the attack on the diplomats.

However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election, has been more circumspect.

He has said the diplomats entered a “sensitive area with a history of confrontations” and without coordinating with the military. He has also said that the facts of the attack on Levine were “unclear”.

Levine has said she was attacked by masked men wearing tzitzit tassels. Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has apologised, saying the “violent rioters” who “brutally attacked” her did not represent the values of Israel.

Settler attacks on the Palestinians are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

(Reporting by Alexander Cornwell; Editing by Tom Hogue, Stephen Coates, Kirsten Donovan)
